title: Crop Care, Nutrition and Health Management

lessons.title: Crop establishment and plant nutrition
lessons.html:
Crop establishment and plant nutrition

Yield potential is set by cultivar, plant population and growing conditions. Management aims to establish a uniform stand and then remove the factors that limit growth: nutrients, water, weeds, pests and diseases.

Establishment

  • Choose cultivars adapted to the region, season length and disease pressure; use seed company trial data.
  • Plant at the recommended window and population for the expected rainfall or irrigation.
  • Ensure good seed-soil contact and correct depth; check planter calibration.
  • Control weeds early; the first weeks after emergence are critical for competition.

Essential plant nutrients

GroupNutrientsTypical deficiency signs
Primary macronutrientsNitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K)N: yellowing of older leaves; P: purpling and poor root growth; K: scorching of leaf margins
SecondaryCalcium, magnesium, sulphurMg: interveinal yellowing of older leaves; S: yellowing of young leaves
MicronutrientsZinc, boron, iron, manganese, copper, molybdenumZn in maize: white bands on young leaves

Soil analysis and fertiliser planning

  1. Take representative soil samples per uniform land, at the correct depth, before the season.
  2. Analyse pH, P, K, Ca, Mg, organic carbon and other parameters at an accredited laboratory.
  3. Correct acidity first: many South African soils, especially in higher-rainfall areas, are acidic; lime raises pH and improves nutrient availability.
  4. Base N, P and K on the yield target and the soil test, using local recommendations.
  5. Split nitrogen applications to match crop uptake and reduce losses.
  6. Use leaf analysis during the season to check nutrient status, especially in orchards.

Fertilisers must be registered under Act 36 of 1947. Over-fertilising wastes money and can pollute water through run-off and leaching.

lessons.title: Water management and crop health
lessons.html:
Water management and crop health

Water management

  • Dryland: conserve rainfall through cover, reduced tillage and weed control; match plant population to expected rainfall.
  • Irrigation: schedule using soil moisture probes, tensiometers or weather-based crop water use rather than fixed calendars.
  • Critical growth stages, such as flowering and grain fill in maize, are most sensitive to water stress.
  • Maintain irrigation systems: check pressure, nozzle wear and uniformity; fix leaks.
  • Water use must comply with the National Water Act 36 of 1998 and any registered allocation.

Crop health

Healthy crops come from combining prevention and monitoring, as in integrated pest management.

  • Scouting: walk fields in a set pattern weekly, record pests, diseases, weeds and nutrient symptoms.
  • Diagnosis: distinguish nutrient deficiency, disease, insect damage, herbicide injury and water stress. Patterns help: a problem following planter rows or the edge of a land suggests a management cause; scattered patches may suggest disease or soil differences.
  • Diseases: fungal (for example grey leaf spot in maize, rust in wheat), bacterial and viral. Manage with resistant cultivars, rotation, residue management and registered fungicides at the right stage.
  • Weeds: integrate cultivation, crop competition, cover crops and herbicides; rotate herbicide modes of action to avoid resistance.

Safe use of agro-chemicals

  • Use only registered products for the crop and problem, at label rates.
  • Respect re-entry and pre-harvest intervals.
  • Ensure operators are trained and equipped with PPE.
  • Record every application for traceability.

Using records

Combine soil tests, scouting records, rainfall and yield data to find the factors that limit yield on each land, and adjust next season's plan.

Key points

  • Establish a uniform stand with adapted cultivars and correct populations.
  • Base fertiliser on soil analysis and yield targets; correct acidity first.
  • Schedule irrigation by soil moisture or crop water use.
  • Scout weekly and diagnose problems carefully before acting.
  • Use registered agro-chemicals safely and record every application.
